output:
Normally, when you send money or record who owns what, one organisation keeps the list. A bank, a registry, a company database. You trust them to keep it honest. A blockchain does the same job without anyone sitting in that chair.

Instead of one master list, thousands of computers each hold a copy. New transactions are gathered into a batch, called a block. The computers check that batch against the rules, agree it is valid, and add it to the end of the chain. Everyone updates their copy at once.

The clever part is how blocks are linked. Each one carries a fingerprint of the block before it. Change an old record, and its fingerprint changes, which breaks every block that follows. The tampering becomes obvious immediately.

Think of a shared notebook where every page is numbered and glued to the last. You cannot quietly tear out page forty without the whole stack falling apart.

That is why people call it tamper-evident rather than unhackable. Nothing stops you writing a bad entry today. It does stop you rewriting yesterday unnoticed. Bitcoin was the first big use, but the idea suits any record many parties need and nobody wants to control alone.

In short, a blockchain is a shared record that many strangers can keep honest together.
